licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: Define the term 'control zone' as used in Canadian airspace classification.
question_text: Unless otherwise specified, a control zone is

choices.label: A
choices.text: the same as a control area.

choices.label: B
choices.text: controlled airspace around an aerodrome that extends vertically from the surface to 3,000 feet AGL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: always Class D airspace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: controlled airspace along airways above 2,200 feet ASL.

explanation: A control zone is controlled airspace established around an aerodrome, extending vertically from the surface up to and including 3,000 feet AGL unless otherwise specified, to protect aircraft during arrival, departure, and circuit operations.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A control area is a distinct airspace category (e.g. terminal control areas, airways) and is not synonymous with a control zone.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A control zone's airspace classification (e.g. Class C, D, or E) depends on the specific zone; it is not always Class D.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: That description resembles a low-level airway/control area, not a control zone, and the vertical limit differs.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), definitions and Designated Airspace Handbook provisions for control zones; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the aerodrome lighting requirements for a night landing.
question_text: Would the Regulations be violated, if a pilot voluntarily landed an aircraft in bright moonlight at an aerodrome where the length of the landing area was indicated by a single row of white lights?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There would be no violation, provided the lights were in the centre of the landing area.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There would be no violation, provided the aeroplane was equipped with a functioning landing light.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, the CAR for aerodrome minimum lighting would have been violated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There would be no violation, provided air to ground communication was available.

explanation: Canadian minimum aerodrome lighting standards for night landings require the landing area to be marked by boundary/edge lighting meeting a specified minimum configuration; a single row of white lights along the landing area's length does not meet that minimum standard, regardless of moonlight, landing light, or radio contact.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Light placement alone does not cure an inadequate lighting configuration.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A functioning landing light on the aircraft does not substitute for required aerodrome ground lighting.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Availability of air-to-ground communication is unrelated to the aerodrome lighting minimum requirement.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), aerodrome minimum lighting requirements for night operations; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the regulatory definition of 'day' used in Canadian air law.
question_text: “Day” in Canada is defined as that period of time between

choices.label: A
choices.text: sunrise and sunset.

choices.label: B
choices.text: one hour before sunrise and one hour after sunset.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the end of morning civil twilight and the beginning of evening civil twilight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the beginning of morning civil twilight and the end of evening civil twilight.

explanation: Canadian aviation regulations define 'day' as the period from the beginning of morning civil twilight to the end of evening civil twilight, which is slightly longer than the plain sunrise-to-sunset interval.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Sunrise-to-sunset omits the civil twilight margin included in the regulatory definition.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The definition is tied to civil twilight, not a fixed one-hour offset from sunrise/sunset.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This reverses the twilight boundary: 'day' begins at the start (not end) of morning twilight and ends at the end (not beginning) of evening twilight.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), definitions section, 'day'; exact CAR reference number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State who may authorize vehicle movement on the movement area of an uncontrolled aerodrome.
question_text: No person shall walk, drive or park a vehicle on any part of an uncontrolled aerodrome used for the movement of aircraft except in accordance with permission given by

choices.label: A
choices.text: the operator of the aerodrome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a qualified representative of a commercial air service being operated from the aerodrome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: a Federal Peace Officer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the aerodrome UNICOM operator.

explanation: The aerodrome operator controls and authorizes access to the movement area of an uncontrolled aerodrome; other parties named in the distractors do not hold this authority by default.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A commercial operator based at the field does not have general authority over aerodrome movement-area access.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A peace officer's role is enforcement, not routine authorization of aerodrome vehicle access.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: UNICOM is a communication facility/service, not an authority that grants aerodrome access permission.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), aerodrome operations — vehicle/pedestrian access; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the fitness-for-duty restriction related to fatigue for flight crew members.
question_text: No person shall fly or attempt to act as a flight crew member of an aircraft if that person

choices.label: A
choices.text: is less than 18 years of age.

choices.label: B
choices.text: has consumed alcohol or drugs 48 hours prior to take-off.

choices.label: C
choices.text: is suffering or is likely to suffer from fatigue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: is over 60 years of age.

explanation: Canadian air law prohibits acting as a flight crew member while suffering, or likely to suffer, from fatigue that could adversely affect performance, as a fitness-for-duty safety requirement.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Age of 18 is not itself the operative restriction described here (licensing has its own age minimums, but this question addresses fitness for duty).
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Canadian alcohol restrictions specify a shorter minimum interval (commonly cited as 12 hours, 'bottle to throttle') rather than 48 hours, and this option is not the rule tested by this question.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: There is no blanket regulatory prohibition on flight crew duty purely for being over 60; this is not the correct fitness-for-duty rule being tested.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), flight crew fitness for duty / fatigue provisions; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State where aerobatic manoeuvres may be conducted.
question_text: A person may conduct aerobatic manoeuvres in an aircraft

choices.label: A
choices.text: only when no passengers are carried.

choices.label: B
choices.text: over a built-up area above 2,000 feet AGL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: within Class F advisory airspace when visibility is 3 miles or greater.

choices.label: D
choices.text: within Class C advisory airspace when the visibility is greater than 1 NM.

explanation: Aerobatic manoeuvres may be conducted within Class F advisory airspace designated for that purpose when flight visibility is at least 3 miles, among other conditions set out in the aerobatics rules.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Carrying passengers is not the operative restriction being tested; the rule concerns airspace and visibility conditions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Aerobatics over a built-up area are generally restricted regardless of altitude; this option misstates the rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Class C advisory airspace' does not correctly describe the designated aerobatics airspace category or its visibility minimum in this rule.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), aerobatic manoeuvres restrictions; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the exception to the standard converging-traffic right-of-way rule based on aircraft category.
question_text: When two aircraft are converging at approximately the same altitude, the aircraft that has the other on its right shall give way except that

choices.label: A
choices.text: aeroplanes shall give way to rotary wing aircraft.

choices.label: B
choices.text: helicopters shall give way to aeroplanes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: gliders shall give way to aeroplanes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft shall give way to airships, gliders and balloons.

explanation: The general 'give way to the aircraft on your right' rule is overridden by a category-based hierarchy: power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft must give way to airships, gliders, and balloons, reflecting the relative manoeuvrability of each category.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: There is no blanket rule that aeroplanes give way to all rotary-wing aircraft; the actual exception is category-based (balloons/gliders/airships over powered aircraft).
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Helicopters are not automatically granted right of way over aeroplanes under this rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The rule is the reverse: powered aeroplanes give way to gliders, not the other way around.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), right-of-way rules — category exception; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session. Mirrors ICAO Annex 2.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: Apply the head-on right-of-way rule.
question_text: When two aircraft are approaching head-on or approximately so and there is danger of collision, each pilot shall

choices.label: A
choices.text: alter heading to the right.

choices.label: B
choices.text: alter heading to the left.

choices.label: C
choices.text: avoid the other by changing altitude.

choices.label: D
choices.text: turn on the anti-collision lights.

explanation: In a head-on or near-head-on encounter with collision risk, each pilot must alter heading to the right, so both aircraft pass on each other's left.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Turning left would keep the aircraft converging rather than diverging.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: There is no rule mandating an altitude change as the primary head-on avoidance action.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Anti-collision lights aid visibility but are not the mandated avoidance manoeuvre.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), right-of-way rules — head-on approach; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session. Mirrors ICAO Annex 2.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the pilot's continuing responsibility to avoid collision regardless of ATC clearance or flight rules.
question_text: Pilots are responsible for taking action as necessary to avoid a collision

choices.label: A
choices.text: unless flying in accordance with an ATC clearance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: only when flying in VFR conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: except when within visual range of the control tower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: at all times.

explanation: The responsibility to avoid collision rests with the pilot at all times, regardless of whether an ATC clearance has been issued, the flight rules in use, or proximity to a control tower — an ATC clearance does not relieve the pilot of this duty.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An ATC clearance does not remove the pilot's own collision-avoidance duty.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The duty applies under both VFR and IFR, not VFR only.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Proximity to a control tower does not suspend the pilot's own responsibility to see and avoid.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), pilot responsibility for collision avoidance; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the minimum altitude and obstacle clearance radius for flight over a built-up area.
question_text: Unless conducting a take-off, approach or landing, no person shall fly an aeroplane over a built-up area unless the aeroplane is operated at an altitude that is not lower than . . . . . above the highest obstacle within a radius of . . . . . from the aircraft.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3,000 ft, 1 mile

explanation: Over a built-up area (outside take-off/approach/landing), the minimum is 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle located within a horizontal radius of 2,000 feet of the aircraft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 500 ft/500 ft understates both the required height and radius for built-up areas.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This reverses the correct figures — the height minimum is 1,000 ft (not 2,000 ft) and the radius is 2,000 ft (not 1,000 ft).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 3,000 ft / 1 mile does not match the built-up-area minimum; those figures do not correspond to this rule.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), minimum altitudes and distances over built-up areas; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the minimum fuel requirement for a day VFR flight (aeroplane, other than ultra-light).
question_text: What is the minimum fuel required on an aeroplane, other than an ultra-light, at the commencement of a day VFR flight? Sufficient fuel to fly to the destination

choices.label: A
choices.text: at minimum cruising speed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: plus 45 minutes at normal cruising speed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: plus 30 minutes at normal cruising speed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: and then to a specified alternate.

explanation: For a day VFR flight in an aeroplane (other than an ultra-light), the required minimum fuel is enough to reach the destination plus 30 minutes at normal cruising speed as a reserve.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The requirement is expressed relative to normal cruising speed reserve time, not 'minimum cruising speed' to destination alone.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 45 minutes reserve is the night VFR (not day VFR) fuel reserve requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A mandatory alternate is not a standard day VFR fuel requirement in this context; that concept applies under different (e.g. IFR) rules.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), fuel requirements — day VFR; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: Interpret standard light-signal meanings issued to aircraft in flight.
question_text: The signal to an aircraft in flight which means “give way to other aircraft and continue circling” is

choices.label: A
choices.text: a steady red light.

choices.label: B
choices.text: a series of green flashes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: an intermittent white light.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a succession of pyrotechnics showing red and green stars on bursting.

explanation: A steady red light directed at an aircraft in flight is the standard signal meaning 'give way to other aircraft and continue circling.'

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A series of green flashes has a different standard meaning (generally related to a return-to-land instruction, not give-way).
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An intermittent white light is not the signal associated with this instruction.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Pyrotechnic red/green star signals are not part of the standard light-gun signal set used for this instruction.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs) / Designated Airspace Handbook, standard light signals to aircraft; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State who may demand production of a CARs-issued licence, permit, or certificate.
question_text: Any person holding a licence, permit or certificate issued under the authority of the CARs shall produce such document for inspection, upon demand by

choices.label: A
choices.text: an airport owner or operator.

choices.label: B
choices.text: any pilot holding a senior licence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: a peace officer, or immigration officer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a pilot holding a valid instructor rating.

explanation: A peace officer or immigration officer has the authority to demand production of a CARs-issued licence, permit, or certificate for inspection.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An airport owner/operator is not granted this specific inspection-demand authority under this rule.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Holding a 'senior' licence does not itself confer authority to demand another pilot's documents.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: An instructor rating does not confer document-inspection authority over other licence holders.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the night-flying recency requirement for carrying passengers at night.
question_text: If your Private Pilot Licence is endorsed for night flying you may carry passengers at night provided you have completed at least . . . . . take-offs and landings by night in the same category and class of aircraft during the . . . . . months immediately preceding the flight.
explanation: To carry passengers at night, a pilot must have completed at least 5 take-offs and landings by night, in the same category and class of aircraft, within the preceding 6 months.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 2 take-offs/landings in 3 months is below the actual recency requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 3 in 4 months does not match the required figures.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 10 in 12 months overstates the requirement; the correct figures are lower.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State what a Special VFR (SVFR) clearance does and does not relieve the pilot of.
question_text: An ATC clearance authorizing SVFR

choices.label: A
choices.text: relieves the pilot of the responsibility for avoiding weather conditions beyond the pilot’s own flying capabilities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: relieves the pilot of the responsibility of avoiding other aircraft.

choices.label: C
choices.text: relieves the pilot of the responsibility of complying with the CARs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: permits a pilot to fly in below VFR weather conditions without complying with instrument flight rules.

explanation: A Special VFR clearance permits flight within a control zone in weather below normal VFR minima, without requiring compliance with instrument flight rules, provided the specific SVFR conditions (e.g. clear of cloud, minimum visibility) are met. It does not relieve the pilot of any other regulatory or safety responsibility.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: SVFR does not relieve the pilot of the personal-limits/weather-capability responsibility — the pilot remains responsible for operating within their own competence.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The pilot remains responsible for collision avoidance under SVFR just as under normal VFR.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An SVFR clearance does not exempt the pilot from CARs compliance generally — only the specific VFR weather-minima aspect is varied.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), Special VFR provisions; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

licence: Recreational Pilot Permit / Private Pilot Licence (Aeroplane)
subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the reference used for selecting VFR cruising altitudes above 3,000 feet AGL in Southern Domestic Airspace.
question_text: In Southern Domestic Airspace, the selection of a cruising altitude above 3,000 feet AGL shall be based on the

choices.label: A
choices.text: true track.

choices.label: B
choices.text: true heading.

choices.label: C
choices.text: magnetic track.

choices.label: D
choices.text: magnetic heading.

explanation: In Southern Domestic Airspace, the semi-circular cruising-altitude rule above 3,000 feet AGL is applied based on magnetic track, not true track or heading.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Southern Domestic Airspace cruising-altitude selection uses magnetic, not true, track.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Heading (the direction the aircraft is pointed) is not the reference used; track (the path over the ground) is.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Magnetic heading is not the correct reference; magnetic track is.

subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the minimum flight visibility for VFR flight in a control area.
question_text: The minimum flight visibility for VFR flight in a control area is

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 mile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 miles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3 miles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 4 miles.

explanation: The minimum flight visibility for VFR flight within a control area is 3 statute miles.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 1 mile is below the VFR control-area visibility minimum.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 2 miles is below the required minimum for this airspace.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 4 miles overstates the requirement; the correct minimum is 3 miles.

subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the correct altimeter-setting procedure for VFR flight within the altimeter setting region.
question_text: When in VFR flight within the altimeter setting region, the altimeter should be set to

choices.label: A
choices.text: the current altimeter setting of the nearest station along the route of flight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the station pressure of the nearest weather reporting station.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the standard altimeter setting.

explanation: Within the altimeter setting region, pilots set the altimeter to the current altimeter setting of the nearest station along the route of flight, updating periodically as more current settings become available.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: 29.92 in. Hg / 1013.2 mb is the standard pressure setting used above the transition altitude (Standard Pressure Region), not the altimeter setting region procedure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Station pressure (uncorrected to sea level) is not what pilots set on the altimeter subscale; the altimeter setting (QNH-equivalent) is used instead.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 'Standard altimeter setting' describes the fixed 29.92 in. Hg reference used in the Standard Pressure Region, not the variable local setting used here.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), altimeter setting procedures — altimeter setting region; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.

learning_objective: Relate a runway number to its approximate magnetic bearing in Southern Domestic Airspace.
question_text: In Southern Domestic Airspace, runway 27 at an aerodrome would have a bearing of approximately
explanation: Runway numbers are derived from the runway's magnetic bearing rounded to the nearest 10 degrees, with the final digit dropped; runway 27 corresponds to an approximate magnetic bearing of 270°M.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Runway numbering is based on magnetic, not true, bearing, and 027° is the reciprocal-direction figure, not 270°.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Runway numbers are based on magnetic bearing (in Southern Domestic Airspace), not true bearing.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 027ºM is the approximate reciprocal runway (runway 09) direction, not runway 27.

subject: Air Law
learning_objective: State the ATC clearance requirement for a VFR flight entering Class C airspace.
question_text: Unless otherwise authorized, a pilot on a VFR flight entering Class C airspace must

choices.label: A
choices.text: request a clearance from the appropriate ATC unit immediately after entering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish radio contact with the appropriate ATC unit only when transiting the associated control zone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: receive a clearance from the appropriate ATC unit prior to entering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contact radar service only when taking off or landing at the associated airport.

explanation: A VFR flight must receive an ATC clearance from the appropriate ATC unit before entering Class C airspace, not merely request one after entry.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Requesting clearance after entering is backwards — clearance must be obtained prior to entry.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Radio contact is required for the airspace generally, not limited to only when transiting an associated control zone.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Radar service contact is not limited to take-off/landing operations at the associated airport; a clearance is needed to enter the airspace at all.

regulation_reference: Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs), Class C airspace VFR clearance requirement; exact CAR section number not independently re-verified this session.
